Key takeaways
•	
Amid macroeconomic uncertainty and rising geopolitical tension, APAC’s IPO 
markets have entered a more selective phase. While deal volume has remained 
steady post-2021, listing value has fallen sharply, reflecting tighter investor 
scrutiny and a higher bar for public market readiness.
•	
India stands out as the most resilient market, with VC- and PE-backed IPOs 
more than doubling from 2022 to 2024. Strong domestic liquidity, stable macro 
conditions, and active pipelines in consumer, fintech, and cleantech continue to 
support public exits.
•	
Meanwhile, Japan has maintained steady IPO volume for profitable midsized 
companies. Investors remain focused on asset-light B2B sectors such as 
healthcare and industrial technology, with institutional support and governance 
reforms reinforcing pricing discipline. South Korea also remains active, 
particularly in healthcare and tech, but faces challenges around post-IPO 
performance and institutional confidence. 
•	
China has seen a sharp decline in sponsor-backed IPOs, driven by weak 
sentiment and regulatory intervention. Listings continue in policy-aligned or 
consumption-driven sectors, but liquidity remains constrained by long lockups 
and foreign investment limits. Southeast Asia remains structurally limited, 
with few scalable, IPO-ready companies and thin capital markets. Public exits 
are rare and largely confined to mid-cap, cash-generative businesses in local 
consumer sectors.
•	
PitchBook’s IPO Predictor highlights healthcare, IT, and consumer sectors as the 
most IPO-ready across APAC, with high-probability candidates concentrated 
in India, Korea, and Japan. Yet the realization of these pipelines will depend on 
company fundamentals, macro timing, and listing venue dynamics.

2
Analyst Note: Opportunities in APAC IPO Markets
APAC IPO market struggling but still primed 
for performance
The uneven recovery of Asia-Pacific (APAC) IPO markets and the highly selective 
pipeline of likely listings highlight a deeper structural transition underway. Rather 
than a temporary lull, we are witnessing a more permanent shift in the ways in 
which companies can exit via public markets. This transition reflects not just cyclical 
headwinds but also fundamental changes in capital markets, investor behavior, and 
regulatory posture across the region.
Liquidity is becoming more concentrated, with only a few exchanges such as India’s 
National Stock Exchange and Japan’s Tokyo Stock Exchange demonstrating the 
depth and resilience to consistently support sponsor-backed IPOs. At the same 
time, regulatory tightening and political sensitivities, particularly in China, have 
constrained cross-border listings and blurred the boundaries between capital 
formation and industrial policy. In parallel, investor expectations have reset, 
prioritizing earnings visibility, governance quality, and capital efficiency over scale 
or market share. These shifts are gradually reshaping the viability of IPOs as a 
primary liquidity channel for private capital.
Nevertheless, the outlook for 2025 is not without opportunity. If realized, even a 
fraction of the current high-probability IPO pipeline—concentrated in sectors like 
healthcare, AI, and consumer platforms—could deliver meaningful DPI across 
the region. But access to that upside will depend less on market timing and more 
on deliberate preparation, policy awareness, and executional discipline. APAC’s 
IPO window has not closed, but it has become narrower, more conditional, and 
structurally differentiated. The path forward belongs not to those waiting for 
sentiment to turn, but to those building for resilience.

Recent IPO trends in APAC
Over the past decade, IPOs have been a cornerstone of APAC’s private capital exit 
landscape and have steadily grown as a proportion of total exits in the region. 
Between 2015 and 2019, the region saw a steady stream of listings at an average 
of about 1,400 IPOs each year, though PE- and VC-backed exits accounted for only 
around 16% of those listings. India contributed outsized exits during sectoral rallies, 
particularly in fintech, energy, and consumer platforms. 
2020-2021 then saw expanded IPO activity due to the liquidity-driven boom in that 
period, with the IPO count reaching 1,303 in 2021 as technology names drove high 
valuations across multiple markets. Alongside that growth, PE- and VC-backed 
companies further expanded their activity levels, with such listings representing 
more than 37% of new listings during those years. Southeast Asia briefly joined the 
wave via landmark SPAC listings such as Grab and Bukalapak, raising expectations of 
a structural listing shift that ultimately proved short-lived as investor focus pivoted 
back to fundamentals.
The post-2021 period marked a sharp correction. While IPO count remained at an 
average of about 1,300 per year between 2022-2024, IPO value fell significantly 
from 2021’s all-time high, reflecting a marked shift in investor sentiment and listing

quality. The retreat in value was driven by multiple factors: rising global interest 
rates, which raised the cost of capital and compressed valuations; macroeconomic 
uncertainty, particularly around inflation and geopolitical risks; and a wider 
recalibration in the public market’s appetite for risk, especially for high-growth, 
loss-making companies. Investor focus pivoted away from revenue growth toward 
profitability and business model durability, thereby narrowing the field of companies 
able to command premium valuations. As a result, although headline IPO activity 
appeared resilient, much of the volume came from smaller, lower-value listings 
concentrated in mature sectors and domestic markets, rather than the blockbuster 
tech or cross-border deals that had defined the 2021 boom.

Macroeconomic overlays continue to shape the IPO calculus. As of early 2025, 
capital outflows from emerging markets and currency volatility across APAC 
(especially in Indonesia, Malaysia, and South Korea) present new headwinds. 
Meanwhile, renewed US-China trade friction under the Trump administration adds 
another layer of policy risk, particularly for export-dependent sectors. IPO viability 
is no longer a function of sector or growth alone; it now depends heavily on a 
company’s ability to meet profitability thresholds, local investor sentiment, and 
macro-political positioning.

6
Analyst Note: Opportunities in APAC IPO Markets
India: An increasingly popular public exit channel
India has emerged as one of the most resilient IPO markets in APAC, benefiting from 
strong domestic liquidity, stable macroeconomic conditions, and a deepening equity 
culture. Within the region, India stands out as the only major market that recorded 
growth in VC- and PE-backed IPO deal count from 2022 to 2024, rising from 22 to 
56 deals, while activity declined elsewhere. This relative resilience reflects India’s 
unique position as one of the few regional ecosystems where IPOs continue to serve 
as a viable exit route for late-stage private capital.

A key driver of this resilience is India’s high retail participation and supportive 
monetary environment, which have allowed its equity markets to outperform global 
peers. The benchmark Sensex and Nifty 50 indexes both posted double-digit gains 
in 2024, buoyed by strong earnings growth in sectors such as banking, energy, and 
consumer services. Additionally, IPO valuations remained relatively stable, with 
median enterprise value (EV)/EBITDA multiples for new listings holding in the 
15x-20x range.

7
Analyst Note: Opportunities in APAC IPO Markets
Consumer and fintech IPOs continue to dominate the landscape, reflecting India’s 
demographic scale and digitization momentum and the increasing monetization of 
daily life via formal financial infrastructure. Key drivers include rising discretionary 
income, widespread mobile adoption, and the success of platforms built around 
embedded financial services and e-commerce ecosystems. Notable exits in 2024 
included Swiggy, which went public at a $9.8 billion valuation and enabled full 
exits for major investors, highlighting that meaningful DPI is achievable through 
public listings in India. Bajaj Housing Finance, another marquee listing, debuted at 
a valuation of $6.5 billion, reinforcing investor appetite for financial services with 
scalable, asset-light models.
Looking ahead, India’s IPO pipeline remains the most active in the region. The 
country’s continued strength will be supported by both macro and structural 
tailwinds: consistent GDP growth, infrastructure-led public investment, 
expanding domestic institutional capital pools, and a visible reallocation of 
global capital away from China. As geopolitical risk premiums shift and capital 
flows adjust, India is increasingly seen as a preferred destination for scalable, 
public-market-ready companies.
Japan: Predictable exits for profitable midsized companies
Despite global volatility and rising investor selectivity, Japan has maintained a 
steady cadence of IPOs, particularly for profitable midsized companies. IPO activity 
peaked in 2021, but deal counts from 2022 to 2024 exceeded pre-2021 levels, 
suggesting a normalization rather than a collapse. Notably, the average post-money 
valuation recovered sharply after the 2022 reset, with 2024 marking the highest 
median post-money valuation for VC- and PE-backed IPOs in over a decade, 
suggesting that public investors remain willing to price up listings that meet their 
profitability and quality benchmarks.
This is especially true in industrials, healthcare, and applied technology, where 
companies tend to be profitable, asset-light, and suited to Japan’s conservative 
investor base. Two recent examples underscore this trend: Kioxia, an IT hardware 
company with a $4.9 billion post-money valuation, and Rigaku, a healthcare 
instrumentation company with a $1.9 billion post-money valuation. Both operate in 
high-skill B2B segments with stable revenue profiles and limited exposure to global 
tech volatility.
Japan’s broader macro environment has further supported IPO feasibility. In 2024, 
the Nikkei 225 hit record highs, aided by corporate governance reform, a weak yen 
supporting exporters, and reallocation of global capital into Japan amid decoupling 
from China. Domestic institutional investors remain the key buyers of IPOs, and their 
focus on earnings quality and risk-adjusted returns has helped reinforce IPO pricing 
discipline and deal stability.

China: A constrained exit channel
For most private capital investors, China’s IPO market has ceased to function as a 
broad-based exit mechanism. From 2023 to 2024, VC-backed and PE-backed IPO 
exits dropped 54% and 73%, respectively, extending a multiyear decline. Several 
factors drove this decline. The macro backdrop remains fragile, shaped by sluggish 
consumer demand, property sector stress, and weak private sector confidence. On 
top of that, IPO activity took another hit in March 2024, when regulators suspended 
the registration-based listing system across most exchanges. Aimed at curbing 
inflated valuations and speculative flows, the move gave the China Securities 
Regulatory Commission tighter control over approvals and led to a wave of delays 
for in-progress deals. Sponsor-backed companies, particularly in high-valuation 
sectors like tech and consumer, have been among the hardest hit.

9
Analyst Note: Opportunities in APAC IPO Markets
Still, not all windows are closed. IPOs in China are still happening, but only under 
specific conditions. Recent listings that did move forward tended to fall into one of 
two camps:
•	
Policy-aligned sectors, such as semiconductors, robotics, and biopharma, where 
state support and capital market reform agendas intersect. Examples include 
Horizon Robotics, with an exit size of $6 billion in October 2024, as well as Beijing 
Tongcheng Bing Technology, with an exit size of $3.3 billion in the same month.
•	
Domestic consumption-driven companies, particularly in politically neutral 
categories like food, beverage, and health & wellness. Recent IPOs, such as CR 
Beverage, highlight how well-positioned consumer brands with local loyalty can 
still go public despite the broader market downturn.

Southeast Asia: IPOs remain the exception, not the norm
Southeast Asia remains the weakest IPO environment among major APAC markets. 
After the 2021 SPAC boom, public exits for PE- and VC-backed companies collapsed. 
Only a handful of deals were recorded in 2024, and median post-money valuations 
remain below 2018-2021 levels. 
The primary challenge facing the region is the inability to scale. Few startups in the 
region are generating the revenues, margins, or corporate governance standards 
that public investors now expect, particularly after the SPAC drawdown and 
the global tech repricing. While capital markets in Indonesia and Malaysia have 
shown signs of life, they have primarily supported local industrial or consumer-
facing businesses, not growth-stage tech companies backed by private capital. 
The Singapore Exchange, once a candidate for regional tech listings, continues to 
face liquidity constraints and weak aftermarket performance. And despite strong 
investor interest, Vietnam remains largely inaccessible for foreign-backed IPOs and 
is still in the early stages of building out institutional-grade capital markets.
That said, the IPO window in Southeast Asia is not entirely closed; it is simply 
narrow. A select group of cash-generating, mid-cap companies with strong 
domestic market positions have successfully gone public, such as Yupi in Indonesia 
and The Thai Credit Retail Bank in Thailand. However, these deals are the exception 
rather than the norm, and they rarely reflect the high-growth, high-burn venture 
model that dominates early-stage investing in the region. In this environment, the 
IPO path exists largely in theory, not in practice, for most early- and growth-stage 
portfolios. Strategic M&A and secondary-led exits remain more realistic avenues 
for liquidity.

South Korea: A steady IPO engine, but bottlenecks remain
South Korea remains one of the most consistent sources of sponsor-backed 
IPOs in APAC, trailing only China in volume. However, the quality and scalability 
of outcomes are increasingly in question. In recent years, South Korea’s IPO 
markets, particularly in the biotech and tech sectors, have drawn criticism for 
poor postlisting performance. Of the 13 biotech firms that listed under Korea’s 
special tech board since 2021, only two have turned profitable, with several 
significantly missing financial forecasts.1 This pattern has raised concerns about 
pricing discipline and earnings transparency, prompting the Financial Services 
Commission to announce a suite of reforms in early 2025 aimed at tightening listing 
standards and boosting market credibility. Key changes include stricter accounting 
standards, more conservative listing reviews, and expanded lockup commitments 
for institutional investors.
1: “NeoImmuneTech Leads Korea’s Biotech Bloodbath as IPO Firms Shed Billions on Failed Promises,” Korea Biomedical Review, Kim Ji-hye, 
February 27, 2025.

12
Analyst Note: Opportunities in APAC IPO Markets
Another key weakness in Korea’s IPO environment is the growing imbalance 
between retail and institutional conviction. While retail oversubscription has fueled 
several headline-grabbing debuts, such as SK IE Technology’s 288x retail bid in 
2021, this enthusiasm often proves short-lived. Postlisting volatility remains high, 
making exits vulnerable to sentiment-driven sell-offs. At the same time, institutional 
investors have become more cautious, particularly with preprofit companies that 
lack visibility on governance and financial discipline. In 2024, institutions recorded 
net selling on the first day for the majority of IPOs—a trend that underscores their 
reluctance to hold positions postoffering.2

What is next for APAC’s IPO market?
In this fragmented landscape, the question is not just which markets are open but 
which companies in which sectors and under what conditions are likely to exit. To 
help answer this, we turn to PitchBook’s IPO prediction model,3 a forward-looking 
tool designed to identify private companies with the highest likelihood of going 
public over the next six to 12 months.
The forecast IPO backlog shows a clear geographic stratification. By country, South 
Korea ranks first, reflecting its active domestic listing culture and continued flow 
of VC- and PE-backed mid-cap companies to the KOSDAQ and main board. While 
concerns around post-IPO performance persist, particularly in biotech and tech, 
Korea remains one of the few APAC markets where sponsor-backed IPOs are both 
frequent and institutionally accepted. 
3: This forecast excludes China.
Still, Korea remains one of the few markets in APAC where IPOs are regularly 
executed by private-capital-backed companies, including in sectors like medtech, 
fintech, and semiconductors. This is because the domestic ecosystem benefits from 
a maturing VC landscape with consistent local follow-on funding and government 
incentives for tech listing pipelines.
Looking ahead, the IPO channel in Korea is likely to remain viable but increasingly 
selective. Companies with strong domestic product-market fit, a clear path to 
profitability, and well-known local backers are best positioned to succeed. However, 
for large, late-stage companies seeking global pricing benchmarks, Korea’s capital 
markets may feel limiting, making dual listings or eventual M&A a more attractive 
long-term route.

India follows, driven by a robust pipeline of consumer-facing and fintech-oriented 
businesses that have benefited from strong domestic demand and public market 
appetite for earnings visibility. Japan lags slightly, as its listing environment 
favors smaller, domestic firms with predictable cash flows—of which fewer are 
institutionally backed. Southeast Asia stands at the bottom of the pack. In Southeast 
Asia, as noted earlier, structural challenges around scale, liquidity, and governance 
readiness limit the pipeline of viable public market exits.
The most IPO-ready companies fall within three key sectors: B2C, healthcare, 
and IT. IPO readiness is driven by the sector’s long-term demographic tailwinds, 
government prioritization, and growing commercial viability across subsegments 
such as biopharma, medtech, and diagnostics, particularly in South Korea. Demand 
for B2C is driven by large, consumption-driven populations, which create fertile 
ground for digital platforms and retail brands. Meanwhile, IT stands out for its 
IPO potential across APAC, regardless of the country. Our IPO prediction model 
shows an equal number of high-probability IT candidates in India, Japan, and South 
Korea, highlighting how digital infrastructure, enterprise software, and applied AI 
are maturing simultaneously across multiple ecosystems. Rather than waiting for 
a broad reopening, investors and founders will need to actively target exits where 
structural support, investor appetite, and market access already align. In this new 
cycle, navigating the IPO path will be less about timing the window and more about 
matching the fundamentals to the right market.
